title: You Were Lied To About Resumes (This Is Why You’re Not Getting Interviews)
description:
If you’ve been told to make your resume “stand out” with design, colors, or fancy formatting… you’ve been lied to.

Most job seekers are following resume advice that sounds good — but is actually costing them interviews.

In this video, I break down what recruiters are actually looking for and why common advice like ATS scores, removing dates, and listing soft skills is hurting your chances.

If your resume isn’t getting results, it’s not because you lack experience — it’s because your value isn’t clear fast enough.

transcript: You've been a lie to about what makes a resume stand out. Run the other way if a career coach tells [music] you that a flashy design resume like this will set you apart because recruiters are not looking for art projects. [music] They are looking for clarity. And if your resume does not make it immediately obvious [music] why you are the right candidate, you are getting skipped. So today, I'm breaking down the most common resume advice that sounds good, [music] but is actually costing you interviews. Hi, I'm Kate Kirchner Career Strategist, Job Search Nerd, and your career bestie. And I've spent the last 20 years helping job seekers actually get interviews. So let's get into it. Let's start with the big one. These overly designed, colorful, graphic-heavy resumes. They look impressive, they feel modern, and they make you think this will stand out. It won't because recruiters are not sitting there admiring your design. They are scanning your resume in seconds trying to answer one simple question. Can this person solve my problem? If your formatting slows them down, hides key information, or makes your experience harder to find, you've already lost. Clean, structured, easy-to-scan resumes win every single time. And it gets worse because some of the most common advice out there is just flat wrong. If a career coach is telling you any of this, don't waste your money. If someone tells you your resume failed an ATS score, run. There is no universal ATS score. Recruiters are not rejecting candidates based on some percentage match. They are reading your resume like a human. The goal is not to beat a system, it is to be clear and aligned. Yes, you should tailor your resume. Yes, you should reorder your bullets so the most relevant ones come first. Yes, you should mirror language from the job description. But do it naturally, not by stuffing keywords everywhere just to try and score higher. If someone tells you to remove dates from your employment history to hide gaps or your age, run even faster. It is okay to leave dates off education if it was decades ago, but never leave dates off your work history. Employers want to see the month and the year. And nothing raises a red flag faster than missing information. The second a recruiter sees missing dates, they start wondering what you're hiding, and now you've lost trust before they've even read your experience. If someone tells you to only include the last 10 years of experience, that can also be wrong. If it's relevant, it belongs. But here's how you do it strategically. Your most recent experience should be detailed and take up the most space. While older, still relevant experience can go into an additional experience section. So you keep the value without taking up the prime real estate. You can list the company, job title, and key skills, technology, certifications, or industry expertise gained from that role. For example, Amazon Customer Service Representative, Zendesk CRM Systems Multichannel Support SLA Adherence. Now, let's talk about soft skills. If someone tells you to add a section that says you're a team player or a hard worker or a great communicator, that does nothing for you because it's generic and also your resume needs to prove it. Instead of saying you're a team player, show it. For example, you could say you collaborated with cross-functional teams across operations and sales to streamline workflows reducing turnaround time by 25%. Or that you partnered with a team to identify process gaps and implemented solutions that increased output by 30%. That's what makes a recruiter believe you. And if someone tells you to dump all your achievements into one little box somewhere on your resume, that's not how recruiters read, they scan. Your impact should be built into each role, not separated from it. Every position should clearly show what you did, how you did it, and the positive results because of it. So if all that advice is wrong, what actually works? Good resume strategy, it's not about tricks, it's [music] not about gaming some system, and it's not about looking different. It is about clarity. [music] Your resume should make it immediately obvious what you do, what you're good at, and why that matters for this role. Because recruiters are not reading carefully, they are [music] scanning quickly. And if your value is not clear fast, you don't get the interview. So let's [music] recap. Over-designed resumes, stressing about ATS scores, removing dates, cutting [music] everything older than 10 years, listing soft skills, and dumping achievements into one section, that's all noise. If your resume isn't getting interviews, [music] it's not because you don't have the experience, it's because your value [clears throat] isn't clear fast enough.
